parsed.study_design: Descriptive case study and action-research programme evaluation using infrastructure surveys, mapping, interviews, and administrative records
parsed.population_and_sample: Residents and community organizations in informal settlements, principally Orangi and 334 surveyed katchi abadis in Karachi, with additional replication sites elsewhere in Pakistan; the 334-settlement survey covered 224,299 houses in 19,463 lanes.
parsed.exposure: OPP–RTI participatory mapping and community–government 'internal–external' service-delivery model, including community financing and construction, technical assistance, government responsibility for trunk infrastructure, and institutional adoption by local authorities.
parsed.outcome: Household and settlement access to sanitation and water infrastructure, including sewer and water-line coverage, household and lane connections, infrastructure investment and costs, maintenance responsibility, and changes in government planning and service provision.
parsed.rationale: Sections III–V report empirical mapping, infrastructure surveys, interviews, programme records, and documented implementation experiences rather than merely presenting a policy argument. The survey of 334 katchi abadis found that 62% of lanes had sewage-disposal facilities and 50% had water lines built through self-help (p. 471), while the Orangi case reports sanitation construction reaching 95,991 houses and institutional changes in planning, financing, and maintenance (pp. 463–478). These outcomes are directly linked to identifiable governance and administrative exposures, including the OPP–RTI community–government model, participatory mapping, and adoption by municipal agencies.
